newsitem.title: GERMANY: Air cargo to benefit from global manufacturing.
newsitem.headline: Air cargo to benefit from global manufacturing.

text.p: The air cargo industry will benefit strongly from a wider global spread of industrial production by German companies, Lufthansa Cargo operations manager, Gerhard Stoenner, told a freight managers congress.

International firms would increasingly use air transport to supply production locations and then to distribute goods to world markets, particularly in Asia, he said in a speech to the annual congress of German shipper association (BVL) in Berlin.
Shorter product life-cycles, round-the-clock production and the potential for built-to-order goods would increase demand for air cargo logistics services, he forecast.

German overseas investments in 1991-94 included 103.5 billion marks ($67.9 billion) by the electronics industry, 92 billion marks by the auto industry and 71.1 billion marks by the machine industry, Stoenner said.
These three industries were key air cargo clients since production was often split between different locations around the world which required rapid and transport links, he noted.
Although air cargo had a share of only 0.1 percent of the German freight market in volume, it had a 10 percent share in value due to the high value of goods transported by air.

The German air cargo market nearly doubled in volume from some 900,000 tonnes in 1986 to more than 1.6 million tonnes in 1995, while Lufthansa increased its Germany air cargo from just over 400,000 tonnes in 1986 to more than 800,000 tonnes last year, he noted. Stoenner said Lufthansa Cargo would offer more international services to meet these changing needs and would establish more airline subsidiaries such as the recently-founded joint venture Lufthansa Cargo India.
Intermodal services such as European rail feeder services to its central Frankfurt hub where a five times a week railfreight services already operates to Milan would be developed, he said.
"We have believed for a long time that we must use rail more strongly, but the railway was not very flexible. Now it has become more flexible," he added.
But it would take another three to four years to get a proper rail feeder system really functioning, he said.
Lufthansa already provides sea-air cargo services for goods such as textiles transported by ship from Asia to the Lufthansa hub in Sharjah, and flown on by the airline to Europe, he added.
The top Lufthansa Cargo destinations were the United States, Sharjah, Hong Kong, Japan, Britain, India, South Korea, Brazil and South Africa, Stoenner said.

Lufthansa transported 36 percent of freight passing through its central Frankfurt hub by freighter and 36 percent as belly cargo in passenger aircraft with the remaining 28 percent arriving and departing by truck, he added.
